system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
diagnosis: Plan-Do-Study-Act quality improvement cycle — Study phase
mechanism: PDSA is an iterative quality-improvement method. In Plan, a team defines the problem, aim, intervention, and measures; in Do, it tests the intervention, preferably on a small scale; in Study, it reviews the prespecified metrics and compares observed results with predictions while identifying problems and lessons; in Act, it uses those lessons to adopt, adapt, abandon, or retest the intervention.
vignette: A hospital unit wants to improve hand-hygiene adherence before central-line access. Baseline adherence is 60%. The team predicts that a new bedside visual reminder will increase adherence to 80%, then tests the reminder for 1 week on a single ward while recording adherence during each observed line access. At the end of the pilot, adherence is 72%, and staff have documented several workflow problems encountered during the test.
lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in this quality-improvement process?
correct: Compare the observed adherence with the predicted result and analyze the workflow problems before deciding how to modify or expand the intervention
distractors: Immediately implement the visual reminder throughout the hospital because adherence improved during the pilot
Redefine the improvement aim and select outcome measures before reviewing the pilot results
Perform a root cause analysis of every prior central-line infection before interpreting the pilot data
Conduct a failure mode and effects analysis only after the reminder has been fully implemented hospital-wide
distractor_notes: Broad implementation is an Act-phase decision that should follow review of what was learned during the pilot; the observed improvement did not meet the prespecified prediction and workflow issues remain.
Defining the aim, intervention, prediction, and metrics belongs to the Plan phase and was already completed before the pilot.
Root cause analysis is a retrospective patient-safety investigation tool for adverse events or near misses; it is not the required next PDSA step after a completed small-scale test.

FMEA is a prospective method used to identify potential process failures before harm occurs. It is not specifically an after-implementation step and does not replace analysis of the current PDSA pilot.
key_expl: The intervention has already been planned and tested, so the team is now in the Study phase of PDSA. The appropriate next action is to review the prespecified measure, compare the observed 72% adherence with the predicted 80%, and examine the workflow problems discovered during the pilot. Those findings then inform the Act phase, in which the team decides whether to adopt, adapt, abandon, or retest the change. Immediate hospital-wide spread would skip the Study phase.
objective: After a small-scale PDSA test is completed, the Study phase requires comparison of observed results with the prediction and analysis of lessons learned before deciding how to adapt or spread the change.

sources.organization: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality
sources.title: The Improvement Cycle: Plan-Do-Study-Act
sources.locator: The cycle has four main parts — Plan, Do, Study, Act
sources.support: AHRQ defines Study as reviewing and monitoring selected metrics, assessing how well the plan worked, and identifying problems and potential solutions; short-cycle small-scale tests allow learning before broader implementation. Act integrates those lessons to determine adaptations and next steps.

sources.support: AHRQ distinguishes retrospective RCA from prospective FMEA: RCA analyzes causes after adverse events or near misses, whereas FMEA prospectively identifies potential process failures and prioritizes them for prevention.
